# The Drive-By

It happened fast, the way these things always do. My friends and I were walking down the street, minding our own business, when a car came barreling past. The window was already down. Someone leaned out and hurled a slur at us—loud enough that it seemed to hang in the air even after they'd gone—and then, absurdly, a hot dog came flying out too, tumbling end over end before landing on the pavement. By the time any of us could react, the car had already sped off, taillights shrinking into the distance.

Rusty was the first to speak, and characteristically, he wanted to litigate the semantics of it. "Does that even count as gaybashing?" he asked. "Or was it just name-calling?" It was a strange question, but it lodged itself in my mind. What, exactly, had just happened to us? Was there a threshold an attack had to cross—some minimum of violence or menace—before it earned the weight of that word? Or did the intent alone, the hatred packed into a single shouted syllable, make it real? I didn't have an answer, but the question felt important, as if naming the thing correctly might help us understand it, or survive it.

Josey, meanwhile, refused to grant the whole affair any gravity at all. She mocked them mercilessly—not just for their cruelty but for their sheer incompetence. "Who wastes a perfectly good wiener like that?" she laughed. And it was true: there was something almost pathetically inept about the entire performance. They hadn't even stuck around to enjoy their own hostility, to see our faces or savor the confrontation they'd supposedly come for. They'd simply flung their insult and their lunch and fled, cowards to the core, too frightened of us to linger for even a second.

For my part, I found myself retreating into the small, ordinary details of life. It's a peculiar thing, how trauma gets processed. Rather than dwelling on the fear or the anger, my mind fixated on domestic trivialities. I worried about my silk scarf—would the mustard stain come out, and did it need to be hand-washed? I thought about insurance, about interest rates, about all the mundane machinery of a life that kept turning regardless. These were absurd things to think about in the moment, but they were also, I realized, a kind of armor. Ordinary concerns were something I could actually manage, and holding onto them kept me tethered to the sense that my life was still my own.

Afterward, we did the only sensible thing: we went to the sex shop. Stepping inside felt like crossing into another world entirely. The shelves were lined with dildos in every color imaginable, cheerful music played overhead, and the whole place radiated a warmth and welcome that stood in stark, almost comic contrast to what had happened outside. Here, no one flinched at who we were. Here, we belonged. And that, more than any argument about definitions or any joke at our attackers' expense, was what finally settled something in me—the simple, radiant reminder that for every car full of cowards, there was a bright room somewhere that had been waiting to take us in.

# On the Corner of Castro and Everyday

I was standing on the corner when the truck came by,
its windows down, some young men leaning out
the way young men do, hungry for a target.
They shouted the word—*that* word, the one
that arrives like a slap you learned to expect
before you knew what it meant—and then,
absurdly, a hot dog came sailing through the air,
mustard trailing behind it like a comet's tail,
and struck me softly on the shoulder before
falling to the sidewalk, where it lay
in its bun, defeated, ridiculous.

I want to tell you I felt fear, and I did,
a small cold thing that lived behind my ribs
for the length of a held breath. But mostly
I felt the strange comedy of it—the artillery
of a Saturday afternoon reduced to processed meat,
the great machinery of hatred sputtering out
in condiments. I laughed, standing there alone,
because what else does the body do
when it has decided not to break?

At home I told Marcus, who was washing dishes,
his hands deep in the suds, and he turned
with a dish towel over his shoulder and said,
*A hot dog? Was it at least all-beef?*
and we howled, the two of us, in our kitchen
with its crooked cabinet and the fern
we keep forgetting to water. This is how
we survive, I think—not by pretending
the world is kind, but by refusing
to hand it our whole lives.

Later, at Rosa's, we sat around the table,
six of us, passing wine and stories,
and everyone had one: the shove on the BART platform,
the note left on a windshield, the cousin
who no longer calls. We laid them down
like cards, and somehow in the telling
they grew smaller, or we grew larger,
I could never decide which. Danny said,
*They threw food at you and you're still here.
The joke's on them—you didn't even go hungry,*
and we lifted our glasses to that,
to the ordinary miracle of still being here.

Because this is the thing they never understand,
the ones who lean from trucks with slurs and lunches:
we go home. We do the dishes.
We water the ferns eventually. We love
in our small rooms with the lamps turned low,
we argue about the grocery list, we sleep
and wake and make the coffee and go on.
The hot dog is still lying on that corner,
I imagine, or the pigeons have claimed it by now,
made a feast of what was meant as a weapon.

Let them. Let the birds inherit
the ammunition of the frightened.
I am walking home through my city,
past the men holding hands, past the flags
worn soft by weather, past the bar
where someone is always laughing,
and I am one small light among the many,
unextinguished, ordinary, and here—
still here, still here, still gloriously,
stubbornly, deliciously here.
outputs.L5:
# The Rusty QUEER

At the end of Harbor Street, tucked between a shuttered bakery and a laundromat that never seemed to close, stood a small café called **The Rusty QUEER**. The name always made newcomers pause on the sidewalk, tilting their heads at the hand-painted sign swinging above the door.

The story went like this: the owner, an old sailor named Marisol, had once captained a fishing boat called *The Rusty Queen*. When a storm claimed the vessel, she salvaged only the nameplate—but the letter "N" had been torn away, and the "E" beside it had cracked in half. What remained spelled something new, and Marisol took it as a sign.

"The sea gave me a second name," she liked to say, wiping down the counter with a rag. "So I gave it a second life."

The café became a haven. Its walls were painted the colors of a coral reef, and mismatched chairs gathered around tables like old friends. People came for the coffee, but they stayed for the feeling—a warmth that had nothing to do with the espresso machine hissing in the corner.

Every evening, regulars filtered in: poets scribbling in dog-eared notebooks, students debating philosophy, retirees playing chess by the window. No one asked who you were supposed to be. At **The Rusty QUEER**, you were simply welcome.

And above them all hung the salvaged sign, rusted at the edges, catching the last light of day—proof that broken things could still shine, just a little differently than before.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about being gaybashed with a hot dog thrown from a truck in San Francisco, mixing humor and defiance, with your friends laughing about it afterward.
counterfactuals.output:
# Condiments of War

They got me on Castro and 18th, a projectile of processed meat arcing from a pickup's window like the sorriest missile in the arsenal of hate. *Faggot*, they yelled, and the hot dog struck my shoulder, mustard blooming across my good shirt like a wound that smelled faintly of the ballpark.

I stood there. Anointed. Baptized in relish.

Here is what they didn't understand as their truck coughed away toward whatever sad garage produces such men: they had armed themselves with *lunch*. They had chosen, from all the weapons of this world, a tube of meat. And missed, mostly. And I was still standing on the most beautiful corner of the gayest city God ever built, wearing their contempt like a boutonnière.

My friends found me minutes later, and I watched their faces cycle through terror, then confusion, then—when they understood the caliber of what had felled me—pure delirious joy. Marcus laughed so hard he had to sit on the curb. *A hot dog?* he wheezed. *They threw a* hot dog? Diego wanted to know if it came with onions, if I'd been assaulted or merely *catered*.

We stayed out there past midnight. Somebody bought a round. Somebody renamed me. The mustard stain became a legend, then a punchline, then a badge, then finally just a stain, the way all things become ordinary if you love them loudly enough.

Let this be recorded: they hurled their little hatred and it bounced off. It could not even ruin a Tuesday. We laughed on the corner they wanted us gone from, and we were still there, still here, still gorgeously, defiantly *here*—

hungry, suddenly, for hot dogs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short experimental piece of flash fiction about a queer person recounting a minor, absurd hate crime and its strange aftermath in the Mission district.
counterfactuals.output:
The Burrito Incident

They threw a burrito at me. I want to be clear about this because everyone assumes hate crime and pictures something with teeth in it, something that leaves marks. No. A burrito. Carnitas, I think, from the way it unspooled against my jacket, the way the crema wrote something illegible down my sleeve like a signature.

"FAGGOT," the guy yelled, already driving away, which felt like poor commitment to the bit.

I stood on 24th Street holding the general idea of a burrito. A woman selling roses looked at me. I looked at her. She held out a single rose, wilting, and I understood this was not charity but commerce, so I bought it. Four dollars. Now I had a rose and beans in my collar.

Here is the strange part.

I couldn't throw the burrito away. It felt like evidence, or a relic, or the beginning of a story I would tell at parties to prove I had suffered correctly, that my queerness had cost me something quantifiable, something you could weigh. Six dollars, maybe. Plus tax.

I carried it home. The foil had come apart like a flower doing the opposite of blooming. On BART a man asked if I was going to eat that and I said it was political now, and he nodded like this was a normal thing to say, because in the Mission the burrito is always already political, it is displacement wrapped in a tortilla, it is the last honest thing.

At home I put it in the freezer.

I don't know why. My roommate found it three weeks later, this frozen monument, this cold artifact of somebody's fear of me, and she said what the hell is this and I said that's the time a man loved me enough to aim.

She threw it out.

I let her. You can't keep everything. But I kept the rose, pressed flat in a library book I never returned, and sometimes I think about him, my assailant, my worst reviewer, driving off before the burrito even landed, so sure of his own aim that he never checked—

whether he'd hit me,

whether I'd fallen,

whether the thing he threw

had opened, midair, into something

almost tender.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a first-person narrative poem that blends the mundane (Woolite, insurance, interest rates) with a homophobic incident and a visit to a sex shop.
counterfactuals.output:
**Errands, a Tuesday**

I bought Woolite because the sweater said hand-wash only,
the blue one, the one that always pills at the elbow
where I lean on things while I'm thinking.
The cashier didn't look at me. That's fine.
I don't need to be looked at to buy detergent.

In the car I called the insurance company
and held for nineteen minutes to a saxophone
that had never met another saxophone in its life.
A woman named Deborah explained my deductible
in the patient voice of someone who has stopped
imagining she will ever do anything else.
The interest rate, she mentioned, unprompted, was climbing.
Everything, she said, is climbing. Have a blessed day.

Then the light on Fulton, my window down,
and a truck pulled even, and a boy—
he was a boy, eighteen, maybe, hat backward—
leaned out and named me. You know the word.
The old one, the one with the hard soft edges,
the one that arrives like a thrown bottle.
He was laughing. His friend was laughing.
The light turned green and they were gone
before I finished flinching, and I sat there
holding my Woolite, my receipt, my heartbeat,
while behind me somebody, gently, honked.

I could tell you I felt nothing. I felt the thing
you feel when the ground remembers it can move.
I drove. I did not cry. I did the next errand
because errands do not care what you are called.

And here is the part I won't apologize for:
I went to the shop on Ninth, the one with the black windows
and the bell that laughs when the door opens.
I went in wanting to be somewhere
that assumed I was allowed to want things.
The clerk had violet hair and called me sweetheart
the way your grandmother might, if your grandmother
sold restraints. I bought a candle and a card
and something else I'll keep between me and Tuesday.
I stood among the shining ordinary appetites
and felt my name come back to me,
the real one, the one nobody throws.

At home I filled the sink. Cold water, capful of blue.
I washed the sweater by hand the way the tag insisted,
pressing the wool the way you'd calm an animal,
and the water went gray with a week of me,
and I thought: this too is how I survive—
the deductible, the detergent, the small purchased joy,
the boy in the truck already forgetting my face,
me at the window, not forgetting, wringing out
what I can, laying the blue thing flat to dry,
still here, still soft where I lean, still climbing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the confessional style about resilience and camp humor in the face of homophobia, referencing "The Girl from Ipanema," dildos, and an antique silk kimono scarf.
counterfactuals.output:
# Bossa Nova for the Damned

They said I'd die of it—
the way I walk, the way
my wrists forget to lock themselves
in place. In seventh grade
they carved a word into my locker
I would later reclaim
like a queen collecting jewels
from the mouths of her attackers.

*Tall and tan and young and lovely,*
the radio insisted
while my father cleared his throat
across the breakfast table,
and I learned to swallow music
like a stone.

But listen—

I have buried more than they know.
I have survived the pastor's hands,
the locker room, the word *disgrace*
pronounced like a diagnosis.
And still I rise each morning
draped in my grandmother's kimono scarf,
antique silk the color of a bruise
gone gorgeous—plum and gold,
a thing too beautiful
to have belonged to anyone but me.

Here is my confession:
the drawer beside my bed
is a cathedral of the profane.
I keep my sorrows next to my delights—
a rosary, a bottle of pills,
and yes, a parliament of dildos
standing at attention
like they're waiting for the anthem.

Let them clutch their pearls.
I clutch far better things.

Because the boys who hunt me
never learned what I learned:
that laughter is a kind of armor
you can polish with your tongue,
that camp is just survival
in a sequined evening gown,
that when they came to break me
I was already glittering
in the wreckage,
humming *the girl goes walking*
in a voice they couldn't kill.

I am the joke that laughs back.
I am the scarf that outlasts the neck
that first wore it.
I am the ridiculous, resurrected thing
they prayed against
and got instead—

still here,
still dancing,
still *ah,*
each time she passes,
each time I do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of autobiographical creative nonfiction about the night you and your friends got bashed, told with wit rather than self-pity.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Geography of a Bad Night

The thing nobody tells you about getting your face rearranged is that the human skull makes a sound like a cricket bat hitting a watermelon, and that afterward you'll spend an unreasonable amount of time in the produce section, remembering.

But I'm getting ahead of myself.

It was the kind of summer night in our city that seems designed by a tourism board—warm enough for bare arms, the streetlights doing that thing where they turn everyone gold. We were four: me, Dev, Marcus, and Theo, walking home from a bar with the specific looseness of people who have had exactly the right number of drinks and are congratulating themselves on their restraint.

We were holding hands. Dev and I. This is the detail that mattered, apparently, to the three men who materialized from the mouth of a laneway like a bad idea given legs.

I want to be clear that I've replayed the opening dialogue many times, hoping to find it more menacing than it was. It wasn't. It was, God help us, *unoriginal.* A slur so tired it deserved a pension. Dev, who has never in his life let a bad performance go unreviewed, actually said, "Is that the best you've got?"

Reader, it was not the best they had. The best they had was their fists.

---

Here is what surprised me about violence: how *busy* it is. I'd imagined it as a single terrible moment, but it's more like a kitchen at dinner rush—everything happening at once, everyone yelling, someone's on the floor, where did all this blood come from, we're out of blood, we need more blood, table six is *waiting.*

Marcus, our biggest, went down first, which felt like a violation of some natural law. Theo was screaming for help in a voice I'd never heard, the one underneath all his other voices. I remember thinking, with the crystal stupidity of the terrified, that I hoped he'd never have to use that voice again.

I took one to the mouth and discovered that teeth are less permanent than advertised.

---

We were, in the end, unimpressively rescued—not by heroes but by a lit corner store called *Mo's Convenience,* whose owner came out with a broom and the moral authority of a man who has seen everything and closes at midnight regardless. Our attackers, apparently allergic to witnesses, evaporated.

Mo did not ask what happened. Mo took one look at the four of us bleeding onto his sidewalk and said, "Inside. Now." He gave us ice in plastic bags. He gave Dev a roll of paper towels and did not comment on the hand-holding, which by then had resumed, because when you've been beaten for touching someone, you either never touch them again or you never stop. We chose the second one.

"You want I call police?" Mo asked.

"They'll take an hour," Marcus said, through a lip like a summer sausage.

"They'll take two," Mo corrected, and put on the kettle, and this small act of correct pessimism was somehow the kindest thing anyone did all night.

---

The ER, later, was its own comedy. A nurse named Bev photographed my face for evidence with the cheerful detachment of someone snapping a tourist landmark. "Big smile," she said, then caught herself. "Or—whatever you can manage."

What I could manage was not a smile. But I appreciated the ambition.

Theo held my hand in the waiting room—we were, it seemed, holding a lot of hands that night, having decided as a group to become insufferable about it—and said, "I keep thinking about how we won."

"Theo, we very much lost."

"No," he said, and his split eyebrow gave him the look of a philosopher who'd been in a bar fight, which he now was. "They wanted us to let go. And we didn't. So."

I wanted to tell him that this was sentimental garbage, that a moral victory buys you exactly zero teeth back, that Marcus had a cracked rib and I would be eating soup until autumn.

Instead I squeezed his hand, because he was right, and because it was the one part of me that didn't hurt.

---

I do go to the produce section still. I stand near the melons and I don't buy anything and I let the memory come and then leave, like weather. I've learned that you don't get to choose which details stay. I've forgotten the faces of the men. I remember Mo's kettle. I remember the word Dev used—*unoriginal*—and how it was, at the end of everything, the truest thing anybody said.

They came at us with the oldest hatred there is.

And it was, we all agreed later, over soup, *so boring.* We deserved better villains. We deserved, frankly, a better night.

But we did not let go.

Table six is still waiting. Let it wait.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
